topics.title: Decimal recap and tenths times tenths

learn.hook: What is a tenth of a tenth? Cut a strip of a square into 10 pieces and you'll see — a hundredth!
points: Fractions with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 are easy decimals: 7/10 = 0.7, 23/100 = 0.23, 405/1000 = 0.405.
A decimal is a sum of place values: 4.372 = 4 + 3/10 + 7/100 + 2/1000.
0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01: in a unit square cut into 10 × 10 boxes, one strip is 0.1 and one small box is 0.01.
So 0.3 × 0.4 is 3 strips × 4 strips = 12 small boxes = 0.12.

example.q: Use the unit square to find 0.3 × 0.4.
steps: Split a unit square into 10 × 10 = 100 small boxes

learn.reallife: A shopkeeper weighing 750 g of tomatoes writes it as 0.75 kg on the bill.

quiz.q: Write 49/1000 as a decimal.
quiz.explain: 49 thousandths: 0.049 (the 0 holds the tenths place).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the zero in the tenths place

steps: There are no hundredths, so write 0 in that place.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out the zero hundredths

quiz.mistake: Drops the zero after the point

quiz.q: What is 0.1 × 0.1?
quiz.explain: A tenth of a tenth is a hundredth: 0.01.
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of multiplying, or keeps only one decimal place

quiz.explain: The overlap is 3 × 4 = 12 boxes, so 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12.
quiz.mistake: Adds the strips instead of multiplying

quiz.q: What is 0.3 × 0.2?
quiz.explain: 3 × 2 = 6 hundredths: 0.06.
quiz.mistake: Keeps only one decimal place

quiz.q: What is 0.7 × 0.8?
quiz.explain: 7 × 8 = 56 hundredths = 0.56.
quiz.mistake: Adds the decimals

quiz.q: Which statement explains why 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01?
options: There is one zero in each number
A tenth of a tenth is a hundredth
quiz.explain: 0.1 × 0.1 means one tenth of 0.1, and 0.1 split into 10 parts gives 0.01.
steps: Split 0.1 into 10 equal parts: each part is 0.01.
So a tenth of a tenth is a hundredth.
Answer: A tenth of a tenth is a hundredth
quiz.mistake: Thinks multiplying always makes a bigger number

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.1. Use a square to show Gappu the truth!
teach.praise: Square-tastic! Gappu sees one tiny box = 0.01.

revise.summary: Fractions with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 are easy to write as decimals, and a decimal is a sum of place values. A unit square shows that 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01, a tenth of a tenth.

traps: Don't forget the zero in the tenths place: 49/1000 = 0.049.
Don't keep only one decimal place: 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06.

learn.hook: Can multiplying make a number SMALLER? With decimals like 0.5, it can — let's see how!
points: Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves the decimal point 1, 2 or 3 places to the right: 3.25 × 100 = 325.
Decimal × whole number: multiply as usual and keep the same number of decimal places: 1.2 × 3 = 3.6.
Decimal × decimal: multiply as whole numbers, then count the decimal places in both numbers and put that many in the answer.
Example: 2.4 × 0.3 → 24 × 3 = 72, with 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places → 0.72.
Multiplying by a decimal less than 1 gives a smaller answer: 8 × 0.5 = 4.

steps: Decimal places: 1 in 2.4 and 1 in 0.3, total 2

learn.reallife: Bills at a vegetable shop multiply decimals all the time: 1.5 kg of tomatoes at ₹40.50 per kg.

learn.hook: If you know 27 × 43 = 1161, you instantly know 2.7 × 4.3, 0.27 × 43 and many more!
points: Use a known product and count decimal places: 27 × 43 = 1161, so 2.7 × 4.3 = 11.61 and 2.7 × 0.43 = 1.161.
If both numbers are more than 1, the product is bigger than both: 1.4 × 1.6 = 2.24.
If both are less than 1, the product is smaller than both, so it is less than 1: 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72.
If one is less than 1 and the other more than 1, the product lies between them: 0.7 × 3.6 = 2.52.
A product of decimals can be a whole number: 2.5 × 0.4 = 1 and 1.25 × 8 = 10.

topics.title: Recurring decimals and families of quotients

learn.hook: Divide 1 by 7 and the digits 142857 repeat forever — and 142857 has a magic trick of its own!
points: Some divisions never end: 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333..., where the 3 repeats forever (a recurring decimal).
1 ÷ 7 = 0.142857142857..., where the block 142857 repeats.
142857 is a cyclic number: × 2 = 285714, × 3 = 428571 — the same digits in a rotated order. And 142857 × 7 = 999999.
One known division gives a family: 156 ÷ 12 = 13, so 15.6 ÷ 12 = 1.3, 156 ÷ 1.2 = 130 and 1.56 ÷ 0.12 = 13.
Find a missing divisor by dividing: 4.8 ÷ ☐ = 0.6, so ☐ = 4.8 ÷ 0.6 = 8.

steps: Dividing by a number 10 times smaller gives an answer 10 times bigger

topics.title: Look before you leap: leap years

learn.hook: The Earth takes about 365.2422 days to go round the Sun — that tiny 0.2422 is why we have 29 February!
points: A year (one trip of the Earth round the Sun) is about 365.2422 days, not exactly 365.
In 4 years the extra part adds up to about 4 × 0.2422 ≈ 0.97 day, so we add one day (29 February) every 4 years: a leap year has 366 days.
Rule: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year ...
... except century years (1900, 2100), which are leap years only if divisible by 400.
So 2000 and 2400 are leap years, but 1900 and 2100 are not.

steps: But it is a century year, so check 400
example.answer: No, 2100 is not a leap year

learn.reallife: Someone born on 29 February celebrates a 'real' birthday only once every 4 years!

learn.hook: Without leap years, Diwali and Holi would slowly slide into different seasons over the centuries!
points: With a leap year every 4 years, 100 years have 100 × 365 + 25 = 36,525 days.
With the century rule, 2001–2100 has 24 leap years: 36,524 days. 400 years have 97 leap years: 400 × 365 + 97 = 1,46,097 days.
Average year = 1,46,097 ÷ 400 = 365.2425 days, very close to the true 365.2422 — off by only about 0.12 day in 400 years.
Without any leap years, the calendar would drift about 24 days every 100 years, and seasons would shift.
Indian luni-solar calendars count Moon months (about 29.5 days). 12 of them are about 354 days, 11 days short of a year, so an extra month (adhik maas) is added about every 2½–3 years.

learn.reallife: Festival dates on Indian calendars move around in the English calendar, but the adhik maas keeps them in the right season.

quiz.explain: 100 years are divisible by 4, but 3 of the 4 century years are not leap years: 100 − 3 = 97.
steps: Century years in 400 years: 4; only the one divisible by 400 is leap.
quiz.mistake: Removes all 4 century years

quiz.q: How many days are there in 400 years with the century rule?
quiz.mistake: Adds 100 leap days

quiz.q: What is the average length of a year with the century rule (1,46,097 days ÷ 400)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the simple every-4-years rule (365.25)

quiz.q: If we never had leap years, about how far would the calendar drift in 100 years?
steps: Each year the calendar falls behind by about 0.2422 day.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the drift is too small to matter

quiz.q: 12 Moon months are about 354 days and a solar year is about 365 days. How many days short are the Moon months?
steps: Solar year ≈ 365 days; 12 Moon months ≈ 354 days.
quiz.mistake: Gives the length of a Moon month

quiz.q: Why do Indian luni-solar calendars add an adhik maas (extra month) now and then?
options: To keep the months and festivals in step with the seasons
To match the number of weeks
quiz.explain: Moon months fall about 11 days behind each year; an extra month catches up.
steps: 12 Moon months fall about 11 days short of a solar year each year.
Over time festivals would drift away from their seasons.
An extra month (adhik maas) catches up.
So it keeps the months and festivals in step with the seasons.
Answer: To keep the months and festivals in step with the seasons
quiz.mistake: Does not link the extra month to the seasons

quiz.q: Over 400 years, the true time is about 1,46,096.88 days, but the calendar has 1,46,097 days. By how much is the calendar ahead?
steps: So the calendar is 0.12 day ahead.
quiz.mistake: Misplaces the decimal point

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why Indian festival dates jump around in the English calendar but stay in the same season. Explain!
teach.praise: Wonderful! Gappu now understands the adhik maas.
teach.nudge: How many days short are 12 Moon months, and what fixes it?

revise.summary: With the century rule, 400 years have 97 leap years and 1,46,097 days, giving an average year of 365.2425 days, very close to the true 365.2422. Indian luni-solar calendars add an extra month (adhik maas) to stay in step with the seasons.
focus: Counting days in 100 and 400 years
Finding the average year length with the century rule
Why calendars drift without leap years
Why adhik maas is added
remember: 400 years: 97 leap years, 400 × 365 + 97 = 1,46,097 days
Average year = 1,46,097 ÷ 400 = 365.2425 days
12 Moon months ≈ 354 days, 11 days short of a year; adhik maas added about every 2½–3 years
traps: Don't remove all 4 century years — 400 years have 97 leap years, not 96.
Don't use 365.25 for the century rule average — it is 365.2425.
Don't think the drift without leap years is too small to matter — it is about 24 days per 100 years.
